claim: Current theories of perceptual inference assume that the brain computes sensory uncertainty instantaneously and independently for each stimulus.
source: Current theories of perceptual inference assume that the brain computes sensory uncertainty instantaneously and independently for each stimulus.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of current theories.

claim: Observers integrate audiovisual inputs weighted by sensory uncertainty estimates that combine information from past and current signals consistent with an optimal Bayesian learner that can be approximated by exponential discounting.
source: Our results show that observers integrate audiovisual inputs weighted by sensory uncertainty estimates that combine information from past and current signals consistent with an optimal Bayesian learner that can be approximated by exponential discounting.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from four psychophysical experiments.

claim: The brain capitalizes on the temporal dynamics of the external world and estimates sensory uncertainty by combining past experiences with new incoming sensory signals.
source: They demonstrate that the brain capitalizes on the temporal dynamics of the external world and estimates sensory uncertainty by combining past experiences with new incoming sensory signals.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental findings across all four experiments.

claim: A more reliable percept is obtained by integrating sensory signals from a common source weighted by their relative reliabilities with less weight assigned to less reliable signals.
source: Most prominently, in multisensory perception, a more reliable or 'Bayes-optimal' percept is obtained by integrating sensory signals that come from a common source weighted by their relative reliabilities with less weight assigned to less reliable signals.
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in multisensory perception in the Introduction.

claim: Sensory uncertainty shapes observers' causal inference and influences whether observers infer that signals come from a common cause.
source: Likewise, sensory uncertainty shapes observers' causal inference. It influences whether observers infer that signals come from a common cause and should hence be integrated or else be processed independently (Aller and Noppeney, 2019; Körding et al., 2007; Rohe et al., 2019; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015b; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015a; Rohe and Noppeney, 2016; Wozny et al., 2010; Acerbi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Human observers are close to optimal in many perceptual tasks and weight signals approximately according to their sensory reliabilities.
source: Indeed, accumulating evidence suggests that human observers are close to optimal in many perceptual tasks (though see Acerbi et al., 2014; Drugowitsch et al., 2016; Shen and Ma, 2016; Meijer et al., 2019) and weight signals approximately according to their sensory reliabilities (Alais and Burr, 2004; Ernst and Banks, 2002; Jacobs, 1999; Knill and Pouget, 2004; van Beers et al., 1999; Drugowitsch et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research, with some caveats noted.

claim: Current theories and experimental approaches generally assume that observers access sensory uncertainty near-instantaneously and independently across briefly presented stimuli.
source: Current theories and experimental approaches generally assume that observers access sensory uncertainty near-instantaneously and independently across briefly (≤200 ms) presented stimuli (Ma and Jazayeri, 2014; Zemel et al., 1998).
evidence: This characterization of current theories is supported by citations.

claim: Theories of probabilistic population coding have suggested that sensory uncertainty may be represented instantaneously in the gain of the neuronal population response.
source: At the neural level, theories of probabilistic population coding have suggested that sensory uncertainty may be represented instantaneously in the gain of the neuronal population response (Ma et al., 2006; Hou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim about neural theories is supported by citations.

claim: In natural environments, sensory noise often evolves at slow timescales.
source: Yet, in our natural environment, sensory noise often evolves at slow timescales. For instance, visual noise slowly varies when walking through a snow storm.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about natural environments with an example provided.

claim: Observers may capitalize on the temporal dynamics of the external world and use the past to inform current estimates of sensory uncertainty.
source: Observers may capitalize on the temporal dynamics of the external world and use the past to inform current estimates of sensory uncertainty.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis to be tested in the study.

claim: More reliable estimates of sensory uncertainty would be obtained by combining past estimates with current sensory inputs as predicted by Bayesian learning.
source: In this alternative account, more reliable estimates of sensory uncertainty would be obtained by combining past estimates with current sensory inputs as predicted by Bayesian learning.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction based on Bayesian learning principles.

claim: Visual signals (clouds of 20 bright dots) were presented every 200 ms for a duration of 32 ms.
source: Visual (V) signals (clouds of 20 bright dots) were presented every 200 ms for a duration of 32 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The cloud's horizontal STD varied over time at a temporal rate of 5 Hz either continuously or discontinuously with intermittent jumps.
source: The cloud's horizontal STD varied over time at this temporal rate of 5 Hz either continuously (experiments 1–3) or discontinuously with intermittent jumps (experiment 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of visual noise.

claim: The location of the sound was sampled from the two possible locations adjacent to the visual cloud's mean location (i.e. ±5° AV spatial disparity).
source: The location of the sound was sampled from the two possible locations adjacent to the visual cloud's mean location (i.e. ±5° AV spatial disparity).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for audiovisual spatial disparity.

claim: The small audiovisual disparity enabled an influence of the visual signal location on the perceived sound location as a function of visual noise.
source: The small audiovisual disparity enabled an influence of the visual signal location on the perceived sound location as a function of visual noise (Alais and Burr, 2004; Battaglia et al., 2003; Meijer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental design, supported by citations.

claim: Observers' visual uncertainty estimate could be quantified in terms of the relative weight of the auditory signal on the perceived sound location with a greater auditory weight indicating that observers estimated a greater visual uncertainty.
source: As a result, observers' visual uncertainty estimate could be quantified in terms of the relative weight of the auditory signal on the perceived sound location with a greater auditory weight indicating that observers estimated a greater visual uncertainty.
evidence: This describes the method for quantifying visual uncertainty estimates.

claim: The temporal evolution of the physical visual noise was designed to be symmetrical for each time period.
source: If observers estimate sensory uncertainty instantaneously, observer's relative auditory weight indices should closely track the visual cloud's STD (Figure 2). By contrast, we observed systematic biases: while the temporal evolution of the physical visual noise was designed to be symmetrical for each time period, we observed a temporal asymmetry for wA in all of the three experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and observed results.

claim: A temporal asymmetry for wA was observed in all three experiments.
source: By contrast, we observed systematic biases: while the temporal evolution of the physical visual noise was designed to be symmetrical for each time period, we observed a temporal asymmetry for wA in all of the three experiments.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding across all three continuous sequence experiments.

claim: For the monotonic sinusoidal sequence, wA was smaller for the 1st half of each period, when visual noise increased, than the 2nd half, when visual noise decreased over time.
source: For the monotonic sinusoidal sequence, wA was smaller for the 1st half of each period, when visual noise increased, than the 2nd half, when visual noise decreased over time (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a specific experimental finding for the sinusoidal sequence, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant main effect of the 1st versus flipped 2nd half period for the sinusoidal sequence (F(1, 24)=12.162, p=0.002, partial η2 = 0.336).
source: These impressions were confirmed statistically in 2 (1st vs. flipped 2nd half) x 9 (bins) repeated measures ANOVAs (Table 1) showing a significant main effect of the 1st versus flipped 2nd half period for the sinusoidal (F(1, 24)=12.162, p=0.002, partial η2 = 0.336)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of the 1st versus flipped 2nd half period for the RW1 sequence (F(1, 32)=14.129, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.306).
source: and the RW1 sequence (F(1, 32)=14.129, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.306).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: For the RW2 sequence, there was a significant interaction (F(4.6, 82.9)=3.385, p=0.010, partial η2 = 0.158).
source: For the RW2 sequence, we observed a significant interaction (F(4.6, 82.9)=3.385, p=0.010, partial η2 = 0.158), because the visual noise did not change monotonically within each half period.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis with an explanation.

claim: The asymmetry in the auditory weights' time course across the three experiments suggested that the visual noise in the past influenced observers' current visual uncertainty estimate.
source: The asymmetry in the auditory weights' time course across the three experiments suggested that the visual noise in the past influenced observers' current visual uncertainty estimate resulting in smaller auditory weights for ascending visual noise and greater auditory weights for descending visual noise.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Both the current visual STD and the difference in STD between the current and the previous bin significantly predicted observers' relative auditory weights for all three sequences.
source: Indeed, both the current visual STD (p<0.001 for all three sequences; Sinusoid: t(24)=15.767, Cohen's d = 3.153; RW1: t(32) = 15.907, Cohen's d = 2.769; RW2: t(18) = 12.978, Cohen's d = 2.977, two sided one-sample t test against zero) and the difference in STD between the current and the previous bin (i.e. Sinusoid t(24) = −3.687, p=0.001, Cohen's d = −0.737; RW1 t(32) = −2.593, p=0.014, Cohen's d = −0.451; RW2 t(18) = -2.395, p=0.028, Cohen's d = −0.549) significantly predicted observers' relative auditory weights
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis across all three continuous sequences.

claim: Observers' visual uncertainty estimates depend not only on the current sensory signal, but also on the recent history of the sensory noise.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that observers' visual uncertainty estimates (as indexed by the relative auditory weights wA) depend not only on the current sensory signal, but also on the recent history of the sensory noise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regression analysis results.

claim: The Bayesian learner estimates visual uncertainty by updating the prior uncertainty estimate obtained from past visual signals with the uncertainty estimate from the current signal.
source: Model 2, the optimal Bayesian learner, estimates visual uncertainty by updating the prior uncertainty estimate obtained from past visual signals with the uncertainty estimate from the current signal.
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: The exponential learner estimates visual uncertainty by exponentially discounting past uncertainty estimates.
source: Model 3, the exponential learner, estimates visual uncertainty by exponentially discounting past uncertainty estimates.
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: The instantaneous learner estimates visual uncertainty independently for each trial as assumed by current standard models.
source: Model 1, the instantaneous learner, estimates visual uncertainty independently for each trial as assumed by current standard models.
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: In the fixed-effects analysis, the Bayesian learner was substantially better than the instantaneous learner across all three experiments.
source: In the fixed-effects analysis (see Table 2 for details), the Bayesian learner was substantially better than the instantaneous learner across all three experiments, but outperformed the exponential learner reliably only in the sinusoidal sequence.
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The random-effects analysis showed a protected exceedance probability that was substantially greater for the Bayesian learner or the exponential learner than for the instantaneous learner.
source: Likewise, the random-effects analysis based on hierarchical Bayesian model selection (Penny et al., 2010; Rigoux et al., 2014) showed a protected exceedance probability that was substantially greater for the Bayesian learner (Sin, RW2) or the exponential learner (RW1, RW2) than for the instantaneous learner (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The direct comparison between the Bayesian and the exponential learner did not provide consistent results across experiments.
source: However, the direct comparison between the Bayesian and the exponential learner did not provide consistent results across experiments.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison results.

claim: Both the Bayesian and the exponential learner accurately reproduced the temporal asymmetry for the auditory weights across all three experiments.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, both the Bayesian and the exponential learner accurately reproduced the temporal asymmetry for the auditory weights across all three experiments.
evidence: This is a qualitative comparison of model predictions with behavioral data, shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The sinusoidal sequence was estimated to change at a faster pace (median κ = 7.4) than the RW1 sequence (median κ = 8.1), but slower than the RW2 sequence (median κ = 6.7).
source: The sinusoidal sequence was estimated to change at a faster pace (median κ = 7.4 across observers, 95% confidence interval, 95% CI [4.8, 10.8] estimated via bootstrapping) than the RW1 sequence (median κ = 8.1, 95% CI [7.0,14.9]), but slower than the RW2 sequence (median κ = 6.7, 95% CI [4.4,11.2])
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian learner model parameter estimation.

claim: The Bayesian learner accurately inferred that visual reliability changed at different pace across the three continuous sequences.
source: indicating that the Bayesian learner accurately inferred that visual reliability changed at different pace across the three continuous sequences (see legend of Figure 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the parameter estimation results.

claim: The learning rates of the exponential learner imply that observers gave the visual signals presented 4.1-5.4 seconds before the current stimulus 5% of the weight they assigned to the current visual signal.
source: Further, the learning rates of the exponential learner imply that observers gave the visual signals presented 4.1 (Sinusoid), 5.4 (RW1), and 4.3 (RW2) seconds before the current stimulus 5% of the weight they assigned to the current visual signal to estimate the visual reliability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the exponential learner parameter estimates.

claim: For all three 'jump positions', wA was significantly smaller for the 1st half of each period, when visual noise increased, than the 2nd half, when visual noise decreased over time.
source: For all three 'jump positions', wA was significantly smaller for the 1st half of each period, when visual noise increased, than the 2nd half, when visual noise decreased over time.
evidence: This is a result from the fourth experiment with discontinuous jumps.

claim: The 3 (jump positions) x 2 (1st vs. flipped 2nd half) x 7 (bins) repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of 1st versus flipped 2nd period's half (F(1,17) = 24.824, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.594).
source: The 3 (jump positions) x 2 (1st vs. flipped 2nd half) x 7 (bins) repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of 1st versus flipped 2nd period's half (F(1,17) = 24.824, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.594), while this factor was not involved in any higher-order interaction (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis for the jump sequence.

claim: In the jump sequence, the current visual STD (t(17) = 11.655, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.747) and the difference between current and previous STD (t(17) = −4.768, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −1.124) significantly predicted the relative auditory weights.
source: Further, in a regression model the current visual STD (t(17) = 11.655, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.747) and the difference between current and previous STD (t(17) = −4.768, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −1.124) significantly predicted the relative auditory weights.
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis for the jump sequence.

claim: Bayesian model comparison using a fixed-effects analysis showed that both the Bayesian learner and the exponential learner substantially outperformed the instantaneous learner in the jump sequence.
source: Bayesian model comparison using a fixed-effects analysis showed that both the Bayesian learner and the exponential learner substantially outperformed the instantaneous learner (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis for the jump sequence.

claim: The Bayesian learner did not provide a better explanation for observers' responses than the exponential learner in the jump sequence (ΔWAIC = +2).
source: However, consistent with our Bayesian model comparison results for the continuous sequences, the Bayesian learner did not provide a better explanation for observers' responses than the exponential learner (ΔWAIC = +2, see Table 2, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis for the jump sequence.

claim: Across four experiments that used continuous and discontinuous sequences of visual noise, the Bayesian or exponential learners outperform the instantaneous learner.
source: In summary, across four experiments that used continuous and discontinuous sequences of visual noise, we have shown that the Bayesian or exponential learners outperform the instantaneous learner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all four experiments.

claim: Across the four experiments, it was not possible to decide whether observers adapted to changes in visual noise according to a Bayesian or an exponential learner.
source: However, across the four experiments we were not able to decide whether observers adapted to changes in visual noise according to a Bayesian or an exponential learner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all four experiments.

claim: The key feature that distinguishes the Bayesian from the exponential learner is that only the Bayesian learner adapts dynamically based on its uncertainty about its visual reliability estimates.
source: The key feature that distinguishes between the Bayesian and the exponential learner is that only the Bayesian learner adapts dynamically based on its uncertainty about its visual reliability estimates.
evidence: This is a theoretical distinction between the two models.

claim: The Bayesian learner should adapt faster than the exponential learner to increases in physical visual noise but slower to decreases in visual noise.
source: As a consequence, the Bayesian learner should adapt faster than the exponential learner to increases in physical visual noise (i.e. spread of the visual cloud) but slower to decreases in visual noise.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the difference between the two models.

claim: Previous research has shown that observers adapt their variance estimates faster for changes from small to large than for changes from large to small variance.
source: Indeed, previous research has shown that observers adapt their variance estimates faster for changes from small to large than for changes from large to small variance (Berniker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The Bayesian learner adapts its visual uncertainty estimates faster than the exponential learner to increases in visual noise, but slower to decreases in visual noise, as shown in simulations.
source: The simulations reveal the characteristic differences in how the Bayesian and the exponential learner adapt their visual uncertainty estimates to increases and decreases in visual noise. As expected, the Bayesian learner adapts its visual uncertainty estimates faster than the exponential learner to increases in visual noise, but slower to decreases in visual noise.
evidence: This is a result from simulation studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: The differences in adaptation between the Bayesian and exponential learner are relatively small, with the difference in mean log likelihood being only −1.82 for the sinusoidal sequence and −2.74 for the jump sequence.
source: Nevertheless, these differences are relatively small, so that the difference in mean log likelihood between the Bayesian and exponential learner is only −1.82 for the sinusoidal sequence and −2.74 for the jump sequence.
evidence: This is a result from simulation studies.

claim: For Gaussian clouds of 20 dots, the instantaneous learner's error in visual uncertainty estimates of 21.7% is reduced to 13.7% and 14.9% for the exponential and Bayesian learners, respectively.
source: For Gaussian clouds of 20 dots, the instantaneous learner's error in the visual uncertainty estimates of 21.7% is reduced to 13.7% and 14.9% for the exponential and Bayesian learners, respectively (with best fitted γ = 0.6, in the sinusoidal sequence).
evidence: This is a result from simulation studies comparing model accuracy.

claim: For Gaussian clouds composed of only five dots, the exponential and Bayesian learners cut down the error by half (46.8% instantaneous learner, 29.5% exponential learner, 23.9% Bayesian learner).
source: For Gaussian clouds composed of only five dots, the exponential and Bayesian learners even cut down the error by half (i.e. 46.8% instantaneous learner, 29.5% exponential learner, 23.9% Bayesian learner, with best fitted γ = 0.7).
evidence: This is a result from simulation studies comparing model accuracy.

claim: Even in situations where observers benefit from combining past with current sensory inputs to obtain more precise uncertainty estimates, the exponential learner is a good approximation of the Bayesian learner.
source: Collectively, these simulation results suggest that even in situations in which observers benefit from combining past with current sensory inputs to obtain more precise uncertainty estimates, the exponential learner is a good approximation of the Bayesian learner, making it challenging to dissociate the two experimentally based on noisy human behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The results challenge classical models of perceptual inference where a perceptual interpretation is obtained using a likelihood that depends solely on the current sensory inputs.
source: The results from our four experiments challenge classical models of perceptual inference where a perceptual interpretation is obtained using a likelihood that depends solely on the current sensory inputs (Ernst and Banks, 2002).
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Classical models implicitly assume that sensory uncertainty is instantaneously and independently accessed from the sensory signals on each trial based on initial calibration of the nervous system.
source: These models implicitly assume that sensory uncertainty (i.e. likelihood variance) is instantaneously and independently accessed from the sensory signals on each trial based on initial calibration of the nervous system (Jacobs and Fine, 1999).
evidence: This is a characterization of classical models, supported by citation.

claim: In the field of cue combination, it is generally assumed that sensory signals are weighted by their uncertainties that are estimated only from the current sensory signals.
source: Most prominently, in the field of cue combination it is generally assumed that sensory signals are weighted by their uncertainties that are estimated only from the current sensory signals (Alais and Burr, 2004; Ernst and Banks, 2002; Jacobs, 1999) (but see Mikula et al., 2018; Triesch et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a characterization of the field, supported by citations.

claim: Human observers integrate inputs weighted by uncertainties that are estimated jointly from past and current sensory signals.
source: By contrast, our results demonstrate that human observers integrate inputs weighted by uncertainties that are estimated jointly from past and current sensory signals.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Across the three continuous and the one discontinuous jump sequences, observers' current visual reliability estimates were influenced by visual inputs that were presented 4–5 s in the past albeit their influence amounted to only 5% of the current visual signals.
source: Across the three continuous and the one discontinuous jump sequences, observers' current visual reliability estimates were influenced by visual inputs that were presented 4–5 s in the past albeit their influence amounted to only 5% of the current visual signals.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Observers adapted their visual uncertainty estimates flexibly according to the rate of change in the visual noise across the experiments.
source: Critically, observers adapted their visual uncertainty estimates flexibly according to the rate of change in the visual noise across the experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Observers' visual reliability estimates relied more strongly on past sensory inputs when the visual noise changed more slowly across time.
source: As predicted by both Bayesian and exponential learning models, observers' visual reliability estimates relied more strongly on past sensory inputs, when the visual noise changed more slowly across time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Observers did not explicitly notice that each of the four experiments was composed of repetitions of temporally symmetric sequence components.
source: While observers did not explicitly notice that each of the four experiments was composed of repetitions of temporally symmetric sequence components, we cannot fully exclude that observers may have implicitly learnt this underlying temporal structure.
evidence: This is a statement about observers' awareness during the experiments.

claim: Implicit or explicit knowledge of the repetitive sequence structure should have given observers the ability to predict and preempt future changes in visual reliability and therefore attenuated the temporal lag of the visual reliability estimates.
source: However, implicit or explicit knowledge of this repetitive sequence structure should have given observers the ability to predict and preempt future changes in visual reliability and therefore attenuated the temporal lag of the visual reliability estimates.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would happen if observers learned the sequence structure.

claim: The experimental choice of repeating the same sequence component over and over again cannot explain the influence of past signals on observers' current reliability estimate, but should have reduced or even abolished it.
source: Put differently, our experimental choice of repeating the same sequence component over and over again in the experiment cannot explain the influence of past signals on observers' current reliability estimate, but should have reduced or even abolished it.
evidence: This is an argument about the experimental design and its implications.

claim: Under circumstances where observers substantially benefit from combining past and current sensory inputs for estimating sensory uncertainty, optimal Bayesian learning can be approximated well by more simple heuristic strategies of exponential discounting.
source: Collectively, our experimental and simulation results suggest that under circumstances where observers substantially benefit from combining past and current sensory inputs for estimating sensory uncertainty, optimal Bayesian learning can be approximated well by more simple heuristic strategies of exponential discounting that update sensory weights with a fixed learning rate irrespective of observers' uncertainty about their visual reliability estimate (Ma and Jazayeri, 2014; Shen and Ma, 2016).
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental and simulation results.

claim: Current theories of probabilistic population coding may need to be extended to accommodate additional influences of past experiences on neural representations of sensory uncertainties.
source: From the perspective of neural coding, our findings suggest that current theories of probabilistic population coding (Beck et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2006; Hou et al., 2019) may need to be extended to accommodate additional influences of past experiences on neural representations of sensory uncertainties.
evidence: This is a theoretical implication of the findings.

claim: The brain may compute sensory uncertainty using strategies of temporal sampling.
source: Alternatively, the brain may compute sensory uncertainty using strategies of temporal sampling (Fiser et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an alternative theoretical possibility mentioned, supported by citation.

claim: Human observers do not access sensory uncertainty instantaneously from the current sensory signals alone, but learn sensory uncertainty over time by combining past experiences and current sensory inputs.
source: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that human observers do not access sensory uncertainty instantaneously from the current sensory signals alone, but learn sensory uncertainty over time by combining past experiences and current sensory inputs as predicted by an optimal Bayesian learner or approximate strategies of exponential discounting.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The influence of past signals on current sensory uncertainty estimates is likely to affect learning not only at slower timescales across trials, but also at faster timescales of evidence accumulation within a trial.
source: This influence of past signals on current sensory uncertainty estimates is likely to affect learning not only at slower timescales across trials (i.e. as shown in this study), but also at faster timescales of evidence accumulation within a trial (Drugowitsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about broader implications of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The findings reveal fundamental principles of how the human brain computes and encodes sensory uncertainty.
source: While our research unravels the impact of prior sensory inputs on uncertainty estimation in a cue combination context, we expect that they reveal fundamental principles of how the human brain computes and encodes sensory uncertainty.
evidence: This is a claim about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: Seventy-six healthy volunteers participated in the study after giving written informed consent.
source: Seventy-six healthy volunteers participated in the study after giving written informed consent (40 female, mean age 25.3 years, range 18–52 years).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: All participants were naïve to the purpose of the study.
source: All participants were naïive to the purpose of the study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The study was approved by the human research review committee of the University of Tuebingen and the research review committee of the University of Birmingham.
source: The study was approved by the human research review committee of the University of Tuebingen (approval number 432 2007 BO1) and the research review committee of the University of Birmingham (approval number ERN_11–0470P).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The visual spatial stimulus was a Gaussian cloud of twenty bright gray dots with 0.56° diameter, vertical STD 1.5°, and luminance 106 cd/m2.
source: The visual spatial stimulus was a Gaussian cloud of twenty bright gray dots (0.56° diameter, vertical STD 1.5°, luminance 106 cd/m2) presented on a dark gray background (luminance 62 cd/m2, i.e. 71% contrast).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The auditory spatial cue was a burst of white noise with a 5 ms on/off ramp.
source: The auditory spatial cue was a burst of white noise with a 5 ms on/off ramp.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: To create a virtual auditory spatial cue, the noise was convolved with spatially specific head-related transfer functions (HRTFs).
source: To create a virtual auditory spatial cue, the noise was convolved with spatially specific head-related transfer functions (HRTFs).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The HRTFs were pseudo-individualized by matching participants' head width, heights, depth, and circumference to the anthropometry of subjects in the CIPIC database.
source: The HRTFs were pseudo-individualized by matching participants' head width, heights, depth, and circumference to the anthropometry of subjects in the CIPIC database (Algazi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by citation.

claim: Participants indicated the location of the sound by pressing one of five spatially corresponding buttons and were instructed to ignore the visual signal.
source: Participants indicated the location of the sound by pressing one of five spatially corresponding buttons and were instructed to ignore the visual signal.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: Participants did not receive any feedback on their localization response.
source: Participants did not receive any feedback on their localization response.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The cloud's location mean was temporally independently resampled from five possible locations (−10°, −5°, 0°, 5°, 10°) on each trial with the inter-trial asynchrony jittered between 1.4 and 2.8 s in steps of 200 ms.
source: The cloud's location mean was temporally independently resampled from five possible locations (−10°, −5°, 0°, 5°, 10°) on each trial with the inter-trial asynchrony jittered between 1.4 and 2.8 s in steps of 200 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The change in the dot's color and the emission of the sound occurred in synchrony to enhance audiovisual binding.
source: The change in the dot's color and the emission of the sound occurred in synchrony to enhance audiovisual binding.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: A session of a sinusoid, RW1, or RW2 sequence included 1676 trials.
source: Generally, a session of a sinusoid, RW1, or RW2 sequence included 1676 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Before the experimental trials, participants practiced the auditory localization task in 25 unimodal auditory trials, 25 audiovisual congruent trials with a single dot as visual spatial cue and 75 trials with stimuli as in the main experiment.
source: Before the experimental trials, participants practiced the auditory localization task in 25 unimodal auditory trials, 25 audiovisual congruent trials with a single dot as visual spatial cue and 75 trials with stimuli as in the main experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The sample sizes of 20–38 participants were based on a pilot experiment, which showed individually significant effects of past visual noise on the weighting of audiovisual spatial signals in 6/6 pilot participants.
source: The sample sizes of 20–38 participants were based on a pilot experiment, which showed individually significant effects of past visual noise on the weighting of audiovisual spatial signals in 6/6 pilot participants.
evidence: This is a justification for the sample size based on pilot data.

claim: Five participants of the sinusoidal and RW1 sequence and two participants from the sinusoidal jump sequence were excluded because their perceived sound location did not depend on the current visual reliability.
source: From these samples, we excluded participants if their perceived sound location did not depend on the current visual reliability (i.e. inclusion criterion p<0.05 in the linear regression; please note that this inclusion criterion is orthogonal to the question of whether participants' visual uncertainty estimate depends on visual signals prior to the current trial). Thus, we excluded five participants of the sinusoidal and RW1 sequence and two participants from the sinusoidal jump sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria and results.

claim: 4000 samples were drawn from four sampling chains with thinning, giving a total of 4000 samples per subject data sets.
source: We sampled 4000 steps from four sampling chains with thinning (only using every fourth sampling to avoid correlations in samples), giving a total of 4000 samples per subject data sets.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling procedure.

claim: Convergence was assessed through scale reduction using criterion R < 1.1.
source: Convergence was assessed through scale reduction (using criterion R < 1.1 [Gelman et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is a description of the convergence assessment method, supported by citation.

claim: Quantitative Bayesian model comparison of the three candidate models was based on the Watanabe-Akaike Information Criterion (WAIC) as an approximation to the out of sample expectation.
source: Quantitative Bayesian model comparison of the three candidate models was based on the Watanabe-Akaike Information Criterion (WAIC) as an approximation to the out of sample expectation (Gelman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the model comparison method, supported by citation.

claim: Parameter recovery was performed and the generating values were recovered with a bias of all parameters smaller than 10%.
source: To test the validity of the models, we performed parameter recovery and were able to recover the generating values with a bias of all parameters smaller than 10% (for full details of bias and variance across parameters, see Appendix 1 and Supplementary file 1-Table 7).
evidence: This is a description of the parameter recovery validation.

claim: To further compare the Bayesian and exponential learner, the choices of 12 subjects were simulated for the continuous sinusoidal and sinusoidal jump sequence using the Bayesian learner model.
source: To further compare the Bayesian and exponential learner and assess whether they can be discriminated experimentally, we simulated the choices of 12 subjects for the continuous sinusoidal and sinusoidal jump sequence using the Bayesian learner model (parameters: σA = 6°, κ = 15, Pcommon = 0.7 and σ0 = 12°).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation procedure.

claim: The number of dots in the visual clouds was reduced from 20 to 5 dots in the simulations to increase observers' uncertainty about their visual reliability estimates.
source: To increase observers' uncertainty about their visual reliability estimates, we reduced the number of dots in the visual clouds from 20 to 5 dots where we ensured that the mean and variance of the five dots corresponded to the experimentally defined visual mean and variance.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation design rationale.

claim: The fitted parameters for the Bayesian model were very close to the parameters used to generate observers' simulated responses.
source: The fitted parameters for the Bayesian model, setBayes were very close to the parameters used to generate observers' simulated responses (sinusoidal sequence, fitted parameters: σA = 6.11°, κ = 17.5, Pcommon = 0.72 and σ0 = 12.4°; sinusoidal jump sequence, fitted parameters: σA = 6.08°, κ = 17.3, Pcommon = 0.71 and σ0 = 12.2°) – thereby providing a simple version of parameter recovery.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation study showing parameter recovery.

claim: The parameters of the exponential model fitted to observers' responses generated from the Bayesian model were very similar to those of the Bayesian learner.
source: The parameters of the exponential model, setExp (fitted to observers' responses generated from the Bayesian model) were very similar to those of the Bayesian learner (sinusoidal sequence: σA = 5.99°, γ = 0.70, Pcommon = 0.61 and σ0 = 12.0°, sinusoidal jump sequence: σA = 6.06°, γ = 0.70, Pcommon = 0.65 and σ0 = 12.0°).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation study showing similarity between models.

claim: The fits to the simulated observers' responses were very close for the Bayesian and exponential models, with mean log likelihood difference of 1.82 for the sinusoidal and 2.74 for the sinusoidal jump sequence.
source: Moreover, the fits to the simulated observers' responses were very close for the two models (Figure 6), with mean log likelihood difference (log(L(resp|setBayes)) – log(L(resp|setExp))) = 1.82 for the sinusoidal and 2.74 for the sinusoidal jump sequence (implying a slightly better fit for the Bayesian learner).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation study comparing model fits, shown in Figure 6.
